quotes.topic: Transposing chord collection by octave drop
quotes.verbatim_quote:
So, let’s drop some shapes down the octave when they start to get a bit too high. This is a much
more practical way to practice the chord shapes for this key:
quotes.why_load_bearing: This establishes the core practical rule for managing fretboard range when transposing chord collections — drop shapes an octave rather than playing uncomfortably high.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
For this exercise, play along with the backing track provided and play through each of the shapes -
any of the shapes in any order will generally sound fine.

Experiment with adding extra notes with your free fingers to the chord voicings for more interest.
You can also play some single lines in between the chord voicings to mix things up.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the method's signature creative drill — using the chord scale as a palette for free improvisation, blending chord voicings with single-note lines, which is the foundation of chord melody style.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The reason:
The ii-V-I progression contains a chord from each harmonic family:

e ii — minor
e V - dominant
e I - major
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the structural logic behind organizing the chord vocabulary around ii-V-I, explaining why mastering these three chord types covers all harmonic situations in jazz.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
To orientate yourself, first play a C major Scale in each fretboard area, then play a ii V I using chord
shapes from the above collections closest to each fretboard area.

Note: I am using the CAGED system to refer to each area of the fretboard.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This establishes the method's fretboard navigation system — anchoring chord collection practice to CAGED positions ensures full-neck coverage for chord melody arranging.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
As covered in module 1, when arranging chord melodies it’s helpful to have the melody mainly on the
top 1st and 2nd strings.

So far, the chord voicings we have learned in this lesson have the highest note on the 1st string.

Now let’s add additional chord collections that have their highest note on the 2nd string.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This introduces a critical doubling of the chord library — having collections with the melody on both the 1st and 2nd strings is essential for practical chord melody arranging.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A chord symbol is an attempt to describe the type of sound produced by a group of notes.

Each symbol you see stands for a formula of intervals:
For example:

Maj7 formula = 1357

So Cmaj7 =CEGB
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the foundational rule for decoding chord symbols, giving students the key to understanding any chord name by its interval formula.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Chords are constructed most often by stacking thirds.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This concise rule is the generative principle behind all chord construction in the method, explaining how triads, seventh chords, and extended jazz chords are all derived.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Slash chords are a way to indicate what note should be in the bass of a chord.
For example: G6/E means to play a G6 chord with an E as the lowest note.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines slash chord notation, which appears throughout the chord collections and is essential for understanding bass voice leading in chord melody arrangements.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A chord’s sound is as much defined by the chords that are around it in the progression, just as much
as the notes of the chord themselves.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This rule establishes context-dependence in chord naming — a foundational concept for arrangers who must choose the correct chord label based on harmonic function, not just pitch content.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In order to fit our chord voicings underneath the melody notes, we need to change the fingering of
the melody to sit on the top 2 (or 3) strings.

Note: it’s ok to occasionally dip down the 3rd or even the 4th string if necessary - don’t get too rigid
about only sticking to 2 strings!
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the central practical rule for chord melody arranging — keeping the melody on the top strings is what makes room for accompanying chord voicings on lower strings.

quotes.topic: Interval label relates to current chord
quotes.verbatim_quote:
The interval number we give a melody note must relate to the current chord in the
progression — NOT the overall key of the progression. This is a common mistake beginner
arrangers often make.

The interval numbers are the chord tone numbers, and could be one of the following:
1, b9, 9, b3, 3, 11, #11, 5,b13, 13, b7, 7
quotes.why_load_bearing: This rule — labeling melody intervals against the current chord, not the key — is the critical analytical step that allows the arranger to select the correct voicing from the chord dictionary.

quotes.topic: Golden rule: interval relates to chord
quotes.verbatim_quote:
The golden rule:

| Always relate the interval to the chord at that point in the chord progression.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This distills the method's core analytical principle into a single actionable rule that governs all voicing selection decisions in chord melody arranging.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A great way to learn these new kinds of chords is by studying minor ii V i progressions, as they
include m7b5 for the ii chord and 7alt for the V chord.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This explains how minor ii-V-i serves as the vehicle for learning the remaining chord sub-types (m7b5 and altered dominants) needed to complete the chord dictionary.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
refer to the intervals as 9, 11, and 13 - as these are more useful interval names for these notes
considering from a chordal point of view, these notes are derived from the 2nd octave of the scale.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Explains the terminology convention students must understand to read chord symbols correctly — why upper extensions are numbered 9, 11, 13 rather than 2, 4, 6.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
On the guitar, there is a difference between the theoretically correct chord and the playable chord.

Often notes can be omitted from the chord shape to get a similar enough sound, but with a much
easier shape.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the practical trade-off at the heart of jazz guitar voicing — dropping theoretically required notes to make chords playable.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Intervals most commonly omitted include the 5th, the root (1st), the 11th, and the 9th. Note though
that even the 3rd and the 7th can be omitted for more complex chords in certain situations as well.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Specifies which chord tones are safe to drop — the operational rule that follows from the omittable-notes principle.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
An extension (sometimes called a ‘natural’ or ‘diatonic’ tension) is an interval of the chord which
naturally occurs in the parent scale of the key of the progression. Extensions are included as part of
the chord name. Examples are G9, G13, and GMaj9.

Altered tensions are notes that are outside the parent scale of the key of the progression, and are
(usually) added in parentheses after the chord name. Examples are GMaj7(#11), G7(b13#9).
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the distinction between extensions and altered tensions — a prerequisite for correctly reading the complex chord symbols used throughout the method.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
You can get very creative with this simple idea. Notice how many different chord voicings I can create
from this G7 shape, simply by adding or adapting notes from the basic shape:
quotes.why_load_bearing: Teaches the method's core voicing-generation technique — deriving a wide range of chords from a single shape by adding or altering notes.
